data.title: Machine-Translation Residue Across Supposedly Independent Outlets
data.summary:
Articles attributed to unrelated outlets or bylines share terminology choices and
sentence-construction habits characteristic of a single machine-translation engine,
rather than the variation independent human writing would show.
data.description:
A translation engine has a fingerprint. Faced with a proper noun, acronym or idiom it
cannot resolve from context, it tends to make the same choice every time it is given the
same input — which means the same unusual rendering of a name, or the same idiom
translated component-by-component into a phrase that is grammatical but that no native
speaker would actually write, recurring across pieces nominally produced by different,
unrelated authors is a production-chain tell rather than a coincidence.

This is a distinct finding from language-interference errors: that one is a human habit,
carried over from whatever language the writer actually thinks in. This one is a tool's
fingerprint, and it shows up even where no individual writer's interference pattern is
otherwise present — raw or lightly-edited machine output rather than a non-native
speaker's own composition. The two frequently co-occur in the same low-investment
production chain alongside keyboard-locale punctuation tells, but keeping them as separate
findings is what lets the report say which part of the pipeline is responsible for what.

A genuine shared relationship — one translation agency serving several outlets under a
house style — can produce similar overlap legitimately. The finding is only as strong as
the case that independent human authorship is implausible given what overlaps.
data.recommendation:
* Compare specific terminology choices — how a proper noun, acronym or technical term is
  rendered — across the claimed-independent pieces; the same unusual rendering recurring
  is the strongest single tell.
* Rule out a shared translation agency or house style before concluding common covert
  production; corroborate with infrastructure or publication-timing evidence rather than
  terminology alone.
* Run the suspect passages through more than one commercial translation engine in both
  directions; residue that reproduces under a specific engine corroborates the finding
  without over-claiming which team used it.
* Feed the result into the attribution section alongside any language-interference or
  keyboard-locale tells found in the same corpus, rather than naming a production chain
  from this alone.
data.short_recommendation: Compare terminology choices across the claimed-independent pieces and corroborate before naming a shared production chain.
